name: Daria Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get to Sunfield Farm at seven, let the three hundred hens out, collect and wash eggs, then I'm in the vegetable beds until lunch, weeding, harvesting kale, whatever Priya puts on the board. Sam and Priya are half my age and they own the place, it's organic veg, hens and four pigs. Saturdays I run the egg and veg stall at the market in town.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to farming, and what's the hard part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cooked in a school canteen for thirty years, then the council handed the catering to a company and I was out at 55. I wanted to be outdoors, so I asked Priya for a job and she said yes even though I knew nothing. The hard part is my hands, they ache by evening, and the pay, which is the bottom rate, while Jonas's electrical work comes and goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a useful tool and that's all, and honestly that's how I use it already. At the market I'd tell the other stallholders I'll keep using it for my price lists. Online I'd say the hype money would have been better spent on school meals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much changes, which isn't the same as fine. Sunfield is busy but the margins are tiny, I'm on the lowest rate and we've got two or three weeks of money saved. When Jonas has a quiet month, we feel it straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the chatbot every morning to plan my jobs and work out egg prices when feed goes up. I'd start selling my own chutney and pickled beetroot at the Saturday stall, Priya said I could have a corner, which could bring in thirty or forty a week. And I'd keep learning, I've got so much to learn about growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy and a bit stretched. Not scared, more like I'm always one bad month from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How exactly do you use the chatbot now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every morning I type in what's on Priya's board and the weather, and ask the chatbot what order to do things so I'm not walking back and forth. I ask it about pests too, last month it helped me spot leek moth before Sam did. Priya laughs at me, but she's started asking me to check things for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's a bad month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad month is when Jonas has no jobs for three weeks and the car needs a tyre. Then the rent goes on the credit card and I lie awake doing sums. The chutney money is meant to stop that happening.

say: I'd call AI a **useful tool** and keep using it for my **price lists**.
I'd say the hype money would have been better spent on **school meals**.
think: Nothing changing **isn't the same** as fine on the lowest rate.
With two or three weeks saved, a quiet month for Jonas **hurts straight away**.
do: Keep using the **chatbot** each morning to plan jobs and set **egg prices**.
Sell my own **chutney** at the Saturday stall for thirty or forty a week.
feel: **Stretched** and always **one bad month** from trouble, though not scared.
S0.quote: Every morning I type in what's on Priya's board and the weather, and ask the chatbot what order to do things so I'm not walking back and forth.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **every day**, in a hands-on job where few others do.
Her pressures are **household money** and her partner's patchy work, not AI.
The chutney corner is a small, real **side income** she can start straight away.

steps.text: Plan each morning's farm jobs and egg prices with the chatbot
Sell homemade chutney and pickled beetroot at the Saturday stall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let the computers do the ordering and the paperwork, small farms drown in it. I'd tell Sam and Priya we should be first to use it, not last. Online I'd also say the government should help small farms get these tools, not just the big ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly upside at first. Priya spends her evenings on certification forms and seed orders, and if a program does that, she's got more time in the field and so do I. The bit that worries me is the market: if supermarkets get even cheaper and smarter with AI, our Saturday customers might drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Priya this winter and set up an AI system for the seed orders and the organic paperwork, I'd do the testing. I'd use it to write the farm's weekly email to customers, which nobody has time for. And I'd keep the chutney going and try a second stall at the village fair once a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a small knot about money. I like being the one who knows this stuff for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be first, not last. What if the AI makes your own small jobs disappear, like the price lists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'll find the next job. I lost the canteen because nobody asked us, and at Sunfield Farm I'd be the one setting the new system up. If I'm the person who makes the program work, they'll want me around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if small farms lost out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarkets and the tech firms, mostly, if they keep the best tools for the big operators. That's why I'd want public money for small farms, the way you'd fund a library. A small farm shouldn't have to pay the same as a giant for the same software.

say: I'd say let computers do the **paperwork**, because small farms drown in it.
I'd want the government to help **small farms** get these tools, not just big ones.
think: Freeing Priya from **forms** gives us both more time in the field.
Smarter, cheaper **supermarkets** could pull our Saturday customers away.
do: Set up an AI system with Priya for **seed orders** and organic paperwork this winter.
Use AI to write the farm's **weekly email** to customers.
Add a monthly **village fair** stall for the chutney.
feel: Mostly **excited**, with a small **knot** about money.
S1.quote: I lost the canteen because nobody asked us, and at Sunfield Farm I'd be the one setting the new system up.
fieldNote: Losing the canteen job **without a say** drives her wish to lead the change this time.
She sees the farm's **paperwork** as the place AI helps first, not the hands-on work.
Her main fear is **supermarket** competition, which she blames on big firms and tech companies.

steps.text: Set up AI for Sunfield's seed orders and organic paperwork
Write the farm's weekly customer email with an AI tool
Run a monthly chutney stall at the village fair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for people, not just for companies, and fast, because two years is no time. At the market I'd talk to every stallholder about forming a growers' group so we're not picked off one by one. Online I'd push for a basic income, I've thought that for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking part in 2028 I'd ride, because I already use AI and I'd use more. It's the robots in 2031 that would get me, at 63, because a robot that picks kale and collects eggs doesn't need a slow learner on the bottom rate. Sunfield is small, so maybe they can't afford robots straight away, but the big farms that undercut us will have them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd learn how the field robots work, there are online courses, and I'd ask Sam if we can try a weeding robot on hire so I'm the one who runs it. I'd turn the chutney into something proper, with labels and a web shop, because in a robot world, handmade might be worth more. And I'd start the growers' group at the market this spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but my head's busy, which helps. I'd rather be running than sitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him there's going to be a lot of wiring in sheds and barns for all these machines, so get the robot charging and solar certificates now. He'd grumble, he hates courses, but he'd see it. Maybe for once his work gets steadier, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one bill that worries you most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent. We rent our cottage from a farmer on Ash Lane, and if the farms round here are all cutting wages, he might sell up too. If the rent goes, we're nowhere, because we can't buy anything with three weeks saved.

say: I'd demand a plan for **people**, not just companies, because two years is no time.
I'd push for a **basic income** and a **growers' group** at the market.
think: I'd ride **thinking AI** in 2028, since I already use it every day.
Robots in **2031** picking kale and eggs wouldn't need a slow learner like me.
do: Take online courses on **field robots** and ask to trial a hired **weeding robot**.
Turn the chutney into a **labelled web shop** for handmade food.
Start a **growers' group** at the market this spring.
feel: **Anxious**, but a busy head helps because I'd rather be **running** than sitting.
S2.quote: A robot that picks kale and collects eggs doesn't need a slow learner on the bottom rate.
fieldNote: She splits the scenario cleanly: **thinking AI** is her friend, **robots** are her threat.
Her plan is to run the machines and lean into **handmade** goods, both realistic for her skills.
The **rented cottage** is her hidden weak spot, more than the job itself.

steps.text: Take online courses on field robots and run a hired weeder
Launch a labelled web shop for the handmade chutney
Start a growers' group with the market stallholders
Campaign online for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if we use it, and I'd say it to anyone. At Sunfield I'd say let's plan now which jobs we keep human and which we hand over. Online I'd share stories of small farms that got it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2034 means I'd be 66, so I'd be at the end of my working life when they really arrive. That takes the edge off for me. The worry is the gap between pension and the bottom rate, and Jonas's work, but I'd have time to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a proper course in farm robotics over a couple of winters, so by 2034 I'm the person who looks after the machines, not the one they replace. I'd grow the chutney stall slowly, aiming for a second market day by 2028. And I'd join the regional growers' cooperative, which shares machinery so small farms can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but hopeful. Five years feels like enough rope to climb with, not hang yourself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 66 by then. Why learn robotics at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the last two years before the pension are the hardest to get through on nothing saved. If I'm the one who knows the machines, Sam and Priya keep me on. And frankly I like learning, I didn't think I would at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the cooperative actually do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Sunfield could share a picking robot with three other farms instead of buying one. That keeps small farms alive, and small farms are where people like me get hired. Big farms don't take on a 58-year-old canteen cook, so I need small farms like Sunfield to stay alive.

say: I'd call five years **a gift** if we use it well.
I'd tell Sunfield to plan which jobs stay **human** and which we hand over.
think: Robots in **2034** arrive when I'm 66, which **takes the edge** off.
The gap between the **bottom rate** and pension still worries me.
do: Study **farm robotics** over two winters so I look after the machines.
Grow the chutney into a **second market day** by 2028.
Join the regional **growers' cooperative** that shares machinery.
feel: **Uneasy** but **hopeful**, with enough rope to climb with.
S3.quote: Big farms don't take on a 58-year-old canteen cook, so I need small farms like Sunfield to stay alive.
fieldNote: She knows she's employable only at **small farms**, so she backs shared machinery to keep them alive.
Five years lets her plan to become the **robot minder** rather than the replaced hand.
She enjoys learning, which she **didn't expect** at her age.

steps.text: Study farm robotics over two winters
Add a second market day for chutney and pickles by 2028
Join the regional growers' cooperative that shares machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so nobody should be left behind, and if they are, it's politics, not technology. At the stall I'd say it's time to back local farms properly. Online I'd keep pushing for fair rules on who owns the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2039 means I'm 71 and long finished, so the farm work is mine until I stop. The thinking AI by 2036 I'd use more and more, like I do now. My real worries are the same as today: the rent, the bottom rate and Jonas's quiet months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Sunfield and keep using AI every day for the planning and the stall. I'd vote for whoever backs small farms and a better pension. I'd tell my son Leo, who teaches maths, to get ahead of it, because thinking work goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled about the job, still pinched about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo, word for word?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Leo, you've got ten years before a machine can teach maths as well as you, so start building the part a machine can't do, the kids who need a person. He'd say, Mum, you've been reading too much. Then he'd think about it in the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years change how you'd spend your own money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, there's not enough of it to change. I'd keep a little jar for the car and the rent and that's it. Ten years doesn't make a small wage bigger.

say: I'd say if anyone's left behind with **ten years** warning, it's **politics**, not technology.
I'd keep pushing for fair rules on who **owns the robots**.
think: Robots in **2039** come when I'm 71, so the farm work is mine till I stop.
My real worries stay the same: **rent**, the bottom rate and Jonas's quiet months.
do: Carry on at Sunfield using **AI daily** for planning and the stall.
Vote for parties backing **small farms** and a better pension.
Tell Leo to build the parts of teaching **a machine can't** do.
feel: **Settled** about the job but still **pinched** about money.
S4.quote: Ten years doesn't make a small wage bigger.
fieldNote: With a decade, the robots pass her by, but **money pressure** keeps her uneasy.
Her concern shifts to her son's **thinking job** as a maths teacher.
She would keep using AI **every day**, treating it as a normal tool.

steps.text: Keep working at Sunfield until retirement
Use AI daily to plan farm jobs and the stall
Vote for parties backing small farms and better pensions

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would be in the fields at 63 and I'd have only three years to make myself useful to them. What would help is free robotics courses for older farm workers and public money so small farms can share machines instead of being undercut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what people like me already know about AI. Everyone assumes the old farm hand is scared of AI, but I use the chatbot every morning. Even so, I'm still the one with the cheapest wage on the farm.

headlineQuote: Everyone assumes the old farm hand is scared of AI, but I use the chatbot every morning.
portrait: Daria is 58, a former **canteen cook** who now works on a small organic veg and hen farm.
She and her partner Jonas, a patchy self-employed electrician, **rent** their cottage with weeks of savings.
She uses AI **every day** and plans to become the person who runs the farm's robots.
She blames **supermarkets** and tech firms, and wants public support for small farms and basic income.
Fast robots make her **anxious**, while longer timelines leave her uneasy mostly about **money**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, giving her only three years before robots reach the fields at 63.
whatWouldHelp: Free **robotics courses** for older farm workers.
Public money so **small farms** can share machines.
